title: Direction & Distance
summary: Compass-walking puzzles: multi-leg journeys with left/right turns, questions on the shortest distance back, the direction faced, the endpoint's bearing from the start, and shadow-based facing. Everything reduces to two signed running totals plus one Pythagoras step, and most answers are 3-4-5 multiples. Shadow questions add one conversion line (morning shadow West, evening shadow East). A written trace of headings and components turns the whole topic into bookkeeping.

subtopics.title: Direction conventions and displacement
subtopics.concept: A direction question is a walk on a plain map. Put North at the top and East on the right. Turn every sentence into one small move, then find the straight line from start to finish. That line is the shortest distance, and it is not the same as the distance the person walked.

formulas.name: Shortest distance
formulas.note: x = net East-West move, y = net North-South move, after cancelling.

formulas.name: Number triples
formulas.note: Doubles and triples of these also work: 6-8-10, 9-12-15.

formulas.name: Diagonal leg
formulas.note: The same rule holds for NW, SE and SW.

tricks.title: Two-line tally
tricks.body: Keep one running total for East-West and one for North-South. Write West and South as minus. The two totals are the whole answer, with no drawing needed.

example.q: A man walks 8 km East, 6 km West and then 3 km East. How far is he from the start, and in which direction?
steps: East-West: $8 - 6 + 3 = 5$.
North-South: 0.

tricks.title: Spot the triple
tricks.body: If the two net moves are 3 and 4, or 5 and 12, or 8 and 15, or 7 and 24 (or their multiples), the answer is the third number. No square root is needed.

example.q: A woman walks 24 km North and then 7 km East. How far is she from the start?
steps: 24 and 7 are the short sides of the 7-24-25 triple.

mistakes.wrong: Adding all the legs when the question asks how far he is from the start.
mistakes.right: Cancel the legs, then use the straight-line formula. Add all the legs only for 'distance walked'.

mistakes.wrong: Treating 'left' as West every time.
mistakes.right: Find which way he faces first. Facing South, left is East.

mistakes.wrong: Turning the page when the walker turns.
mistakes.right: Keep North at the top all the time. Only the walker turns.

mistakes.wrong: Splitting a $k\sqrt{2}$ diagonal leg into $k\sqrt{2}$ on each side.
mistakes.right: A $k\sqrt{2}$ diagonal leg is $k$ on each side.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting to cancel opposite legs.
mistakes.right: Pair North with South and East with West before any square root.

subtopics.notes:
### The four directions
Draw a map with **North at the top** and **East on the right**. South is at the bottom. West is on the left.

Between them sit four mixed directions: North-East, North-West, South-East and South-West. "Towards the sunrise" means East. "Towards the sunset" means West.

> **Rule:** Draw the map once, with North up. Never turn the page when the walker turns.

### Left and right belong to the walker
A left turn does not mean "West". It means "to the left of the way he faces now".

| The walker faces | Left is | Right is |
|---|---|---|
| North | West | East |
| South | East | West |
| East | North | South |
| West | South | North |

A man walks North and turns left. He now walks West. The same left turn from South would send him East.

> **Watch:** "Left = West" is true only when the walker faces North. Check the table for every turn.

### Turn each sentence into a move
Start at the middle of the map. Each sentence moves you. Keep a running tally on two lines: East-West and North-South.

- East and North count as plus.
- West and South count as minus.

Example: "8 km East, 6 km West, then 3 km East." The East-West line is $8 - 6 + 3 = 5$. He is 5 km East of the start.

### Cancel opposite legs first
A leg is one straight part of the walk. Two legs that go opposite ways on the same line cancel each other.

A man walks 15 km North, 9 km East, then 15 km South. The 15 North and 15 South cancel. Only 9 km East is left.

> **Tip:** Cancel first, then calculate. Most questions hide two or three cancellations.

### Shortest distance
The shortest distance is the straight line from start to finish. After cancelling, you have a net East move and a net North move. They are the two short sides of a right triangle.

$$d = \sqrt{(\text{net East})^2 + (\text{net North})^2}$$

Example: 3 km East and 4 km North gives $\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$ km.

Most exam answers come from these number triples:

| Short sides | Straight line |
|---|---|
| 3 and 4 | 5 |
| 5 and 12 | 13 |
| 8 and 15 | 17 |
| 7 and 24 | 25 |

Doubles and triples also work: 6 and 8 give 10, and 9 and 12 give 15.

### Diagonal legs
A leg such as "5$\sqrt{2}$ km North-East" is a slanting step. It moves 5 km North and 5 km East at the same time.

- North-East: $k$ North and $k$ East.
- North-West: $k$ North and $k$ West.
- South-East: $k$ South and $k$ East.
- South-West: $k$ South and $k$ West.

Example: 5$\sqrt{2}$ km North-East, then 5$\sqrt{2}$ km North-West. The East and West parts cancel. The North parts add up to 10 km.

### Distance walked or shortest distance
Read the last line twice. Each phrase asks for a different number.

| The question asks | Find |
|---|---|
| How far is he from the start? | Straight line (Pythagoras) |
| How much distance did he walk? | Add all the legs |
| How much shorter is the direct path? | Total walked minus straight line |
| In which direction is he from the start? | Compass word of the net moves |

> **Watch:** The walked distance and the straight line are always two different options. Do not pick the wrong one.

patterns.name: Straight line after two perpendicular legs
patterns.howToSpot: The legs run North-South and East-West. The question asks how far he is from the starting point.
steps: Write each leg as an East-West move or a North-South move.
Cancel opposite legs and find the net East and net North.
Look for a number triple (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17).
Otherwise apply the square root formula.
patterns.why: The two net moves are the short sides of a right triangle. The straight line home is its longest side.

example.q: A man walks 9 km East and then 12 km North. How far is he from the starting point?
steps: Net moves: 9 km East and 12 km North.
9 and 12 are 3 times 3 and 3 times 4.
Distance = $3 \times 5 = 15$ km.

patterns.name: Legs that cancel out
patterns.howToSpot: The path doubles back. A leg North is followed by a leg South, or East by West.
steps: Pair each leg with the leg that goes the opposite way.
Cancel the pairs. Subtract the smaller from the larger.
Use only what is left to find the distance.
patterns.why: Only the start and the end matter. Retraced legs add nothing to the gap.

example.q: A cyclist rides 15 km West, 6 km North, 15 km East and then 2 km North. How far is he from the starting point?
steps: 15 km West and 15 km East cancel.
North legs add up: $6 + 2 = 8$ km.
Only 8 km North is left.

patterns.name: Diagonal legs written with root 2
patterns.howToSpot: A leg is written as $k\sqrt{2}$ km towards North-East, North-West, South-East or South-West.
patterns.formula: k\sqrt{2}\ \text{diagonal} = k\ \text{on each of two sides}
steps: Split each diagonal leg into two equal parts of $k$.
Add up the East-West parts and the North-South parts.
Find the straight line from the net moves.
patterns.why: A diagonal step of $k\sqrt{2}$ is the slanting side of a right triangle with two sides of $k$.

example.q: A man walks $8\sqrt{2}$ km North-East and then 2 km West. How far is he from the starting point?
steps: North-East leg: 8 km East and 8 km North.
Then 2 km West: East part is $8 - 2 = 6$ km.
Net moves 6 and 8, so the distance is 10 km.

patterns.name: Total distance walked
patterns.howToSpot: The question says "how much distance did he cover or walk" for a path that ends away from the start.
steps: Ignore all directions.
Add the length of every leg.
Do not use Pythagoras.
patterns.why: Distance walked counts every step. The straight line counts only the gap between start and end.

example.q: A man walks 9 km East and then 12 km North. What total distance does he cover?
steps: Add the two legs.

patterns.name: Left and right turns, then the gap
patterns.howToSpot: The walker turns left or right in the middle of the walk. The straight-line distance is asked.
steps: Note the way he faces at the start.
After each turn, use the left-right table to find the new direction.
Turn each leg into a North, South, East or West move.
Find the net moves and the straight line.
patterns.why: The map never turns, so each new direction must be found one turn at a time.

example.q: Sanjay walks 8 km North. He turns right and walks 6 km. How far is he from the start?
steps: Facing North, right is East.
Moves: 8 km North and 6 km East.
6 and 8 give the triple 6-8-10.

patterns.name: How much shorter is the straight path
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks how much distance would be saved by walking straight instead.
steps: Add all the legs to get the total walked.
Find the straight line by Pythagoras.
Subtract the straight line from the total.
patterns.why: The saving is the gap between the two numbers you already know how to find.

example.q: A man walks 9 km East and then 12 km North. How much shorter is the direct path from start to finish?
steps: Total walked: 9 + 12 = 21 km.
Straight line: 15 km.

revision: North is up and East is right. The page never turns.
Left and right depend on the way the walker faces.
Tally East-West and North-South. West and South are minus.
Cancel opposite legs before any calculation.
Straight line: $\sqrt{(\text{East})^2 + (\text{North})^2}$.
A diagonal leg of $k\sqrt{2}$ is $k$ on each of its two sides.

subtopics.title: Direction faced and net direction
subtopics.concept: Two kinds of question live here. One asks which way a person faces after some turns. The other asks in which direction the end point lies from the start. Write the direction after every turn, and never trust your memory over three turns.

formulas.name: Clockwise cycle
formulas.note: Every right turn moves one step along this circle.

formulas.name: Anticlockwise cycle
formulas.note: Every left turn moves one step along this circle.

formulas.name: Reading the end point
formulas.note: x is the net East move and y is the net North move. Their signs give the compass word.

tricks.title: Write the direction after every turn
tricks.body: After each turn, write one letter: N, E, S or W. Overwrite the old letter. Three written letters are safer than one long chain in your head.

example.q: Facing West, a man turns 90 degrees clockwise and then 180 degrees anticlockwise. Which way does he face?
steps: West, then 90 clockwise: North.
180 either way: South.

tricks.title: Reverse the pair, flip the word
tricks.body: If B is North-East of A, then A is South-West of B. The mixed words flip together.

example.q: B is 3 km East and 4 km North of A. In which direction is A from B?
steps: B from A is North-East.
Reverse the pair: A from B is South-West.

mistakes.wrong: Using 'left = West' without checking which way he faces.
mistakes.right: Check the table of turns. Left of South is East.

mistakes.wrong: Counting an about-turn as one quarter-turn.
mistakes.right: An about-turn is two quarter-turns, 180 degrees.

mistakes.wrong: Giving the facing when the question asks the direction from the start.
mistakes.right: Underline the last line. 'Facing' and 'direction from the start' are different answers.

mistakes.wrong: Reading the end direction from the distances instead of the net moves.
mistakes.right: Use the signs of the net East and North moves.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting to flip the answer when the pair is reversed.
mistakes.right: North-East becomes South-West when the two people swap places.

subtopics.notes:
### Which way is he facing now
Only the turns matter here. The distances are decoration.

A right turn of 90 degrees moves you one step **clockwise** on this circle: North, East, South, West, and back to North. A left turn moves one step the other way.

| Start facing | After a right turn | After a left turn |
|---|---|---|
| North | East | West |
| East | South | North |
| South | West | East |
| West | North | South |

> **Rule:** Right is one step clockwise. Left is one step back. An about-turn (180 degrees) is two steps.

### Count the quarter-turns
One quarter-turn is 90 degrees. Count rights as plus and lefts as minus. Add them.

Example: facing West, a man turns 90 degrees anticlockwise, then 270 degrees clockwise. That is $-1 + 3 = +2$ quarter-turns. Two steps clockwise from West is **East**.

Four quarter-turns bring you back to where you started. So cross out 4 whenever it appears.

> **Tip:** 270 degrees clockwise is the same as 90 degrees anticlockwise. Both end in the same place.

### Which direction is the end point
Now the path matters and the facing does not. Find the net East move and the net North move. Then read the compass from their signs.

| East move | North move | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| plus | plus | North-East |
| minus | plus | North-West |
| plus | minus | South-East |
| minus | minus | South-West |

If one move is zero, use one word only. A net move of 4 km North and 0 East is simply **North**.

"Direction of B from A" means: stand at A, look at B. Swap the two people and the answer flips. North-East becomes South-West.

### Turns in the middle of a walk
"Walks 5 km, turns left, walks 3 km." The word "left" depends on the way he walks now. So track the direction leg by leg.

Example: a man walks North, turns right and walks 4 km, then turns left and walks 3 km. Right of North is East. Left of East is North. He moves 4 km East and 3 km North. He ends **North-East** of the start.

### Turning back
"Turns back", "returns" and "about-turn" all mean 180 degrees. He now faces the opposite way.

A man walks 6 km East, then turns back and walks 2 km. He faces West. He is $6 - 2 = 4$ km East of the start.

> **Watch:** The end direction and the facing direction are two different answers. Read which one the question wants.

### Questions that ask both
A hard question gives turns and then asks the direction of the end point. Keep two lists.

1. List one: the direction he faces after each turn.
2. List two: the net East and North moves.

Do not read one list from the other. A quick picture check helps. If he ended North and East of the start, he cannot be South-West.

patterns.name: Net quarter-turns for the final facing
patterns.howToSpot: A starting direction and a list of turns are given. The question asks which way he faces now.
steps: Count a right turn as +1, a left turn as -1 and an about-turn as 2.
Add them up and drop any 4.
Move that many steps clockwise from the start.
patterns.why: Each turn is a quarter of a full circle, and four quarters bring you home.

example.q: A man faces South. He turns 90 degrees clockwise, then 180 degrees, then 90 degrees anticlockwise. Which way does he face now?
steps: Total: +2.
Two steps clockwise from South: West, then North.

patterns.name: Direction of the end point from the start
patterns.howToSpot: A path is given. The question asks in which direction the finish is from the starting point.
steps: Find the net East-West move and the net North-South move.
Look at the sign of each.
Join the two words. Use one word if a move is zero.
patterns.why: The direction of the end point is the compass word of the net move.

example.q: Priya walks 6 km North, 2 km East, 9 km South and then 2 km East. In which direction is she from the starting point?
steps: East-West: 2 + 2 = 4 km East.
North-South: 6 - 9 = 3 km South.
East and South make South-East.

patterns.name: Left and right turns in the middle
patterns.howToSpot: The path has turns such as "turns left" or "turns right", and the final direction is asked.
steps: Write the direction he faces at the start.
After each turn, write the new direction. Overwrite the old letter.
The last letter is the final direction.
patterns.why: The words left and right change meaning with every turn, so only a written chain is safe.

example.q: Walking East, Arun turns right, walks 4 km, and then turns right again. Which way does he face now?
steps: Start: East.
Right turn: South.
Right turn again: West.

patterns.name: Turning back and returning
patterns.howToSpot: The path says "turns back", "returns" or "retraces" in the middle.
steps: An about-turn makes him face the opposite direction.
A new leg after it cancels part of the old one.
Finish the rest of the path and find the net moves.
patterns.why: Turning back sends him along the same line the other way, so the new leg reduces the gap.

example.q: A man walks 8 km North, turns back and walks 4 km, and then turns left and walks 3 km. How far and in which direction is he from the start?
steps: Turning back: he faces South and walks 4 km. North-South: 8 - 4 = 4 km North.
Left of South is East. He walks 3 km East.
Net moves 3 East and 4 North give 5 km, towards North-East.

patterns.name: Facing and end point together
patterns.howToSpot: A path with several turns is given. It asks for the distance and direction from the start.
steps: Track the facing after each turn in list one.
Turn each leg into a North, South, East or West move.
Find the net moves, then the distance and the compass word.
patterns.why: The turns give the direction of each leg. The legs then give the net move.

example.q: Deepa faces West and walks 4 km. She turns right and walks 3 km, and then turns right again and walks 4 km. How far and in which direction is she from the start?
steps: West 4 km, then right turn: North 3 km, then right turn: East 4 km.
East-West: 4 West and 4 East cancel.
Only 3 km North is left.

revision: Right turn: one step clockwise on N, E, S, W. Left turn: one step back.
An about-turn is two steps. Four quarter-turns are a full circle.
Net quarter-turns = rights minus lefts.
Direction of the end point: signs of the net East and North moves.
'B from A' means stand at A and look at B. Reversing the pair flips the word.
Track the facing leg by leg when turns come in the middle.
Facing and end direction are two different answers.

subtopics.title: Shadow questions
subtopics.concept: The sun fixes the direction of every shadow. In the morning the sun is in the East, so shadows point West. In the evening the sun is in the West, so shadows point East. Turn the shadow words into a sentence about which way the person faces, then finish the question.

tricks.title: Change the shadow into a facing first
tricks.body: Before any other step, rewrite the sentence as a facing sentence. Morning and shadow behind him means he faces East. Evening and shadow in front means he faces East.

example.q: In the morning, a boy's shadow falls on his left. Which way does he face?
steps: Morning shadow points West.
West is on his left when he faces North.

mistakes.wrong: Using the evening shadow direction in a morning question.
mistakes.right: Write 'morning: shadow West' or 'evening: shadow East' first.

mistakes.wrong: Giving the shadow's direction when the question asks the person's facing.
mistakes.right: The shadow and the facing are two different arrows. Answer the one asked.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting that left and right change when the facing changes.
mistakes.right: Use the body map for each facing.

mistakes.wrong: Treating back to back as facing the same way.
mistakes.right: Back to back means the two people face opposite ways.

mistakes.wrong: Treating 'away from the shadow' as the shadow's direction.
mistakes.right: Away from it means the opposite direction.

subtopics.notes:
### The sun points the shadow
A shadow always falls away from the sun. So the sun does the pointing for you.

| Time | Sun is in the | Shadow points |
|---|---|---|
| Morning (sunrise) | East | West |
| Evening (sunset) | West | East |

At noon in India, the shadow points roughly North. Most questions avoid noon.

> **Rule:** Write "morning: shadow West" or "evening: shadow East" before you read anything else.

### Where the shadow falls on the body
A person faces some direction. The shadow can fall in front, behind, on the left or on the right.

- Shadow in front: he faces the same way as the shadow.
- Shadow behind: he faces the opposite way.
- Shadow on the left or right: he faces a direction at right angles to the shadow.

Example: morning, shadow falls in front of him. The shadow points West, so he faces **West**. If it falls behind him, he faces East.

### Left and right shadows
Use the body map. It tells you what lies on the left and right for each facing.

| He faces | Left is | Right is |
|---|---|---|
| North | West | East |
| South | East | West |
| East | North | South |
| West | South | North |

Example: morning, shadow falls on his right. The shadow points West. West is on his right when he faces South. So he faces **South**.

> **Tip:** For a morning shadow, left means facing North and right means facing South. For an evening shadow, left means South and right means North.

### Two people, back to back
Back to back means the two people face opposite ways. Find one person's facing from the shadow. The other faces the opposite way.

Example: evening, Rohit's shadow falls on his left. The shadow points East. So Rohit faces South. His partner stands back to back with him, so he faces **North**.

### Four pictures to learn
Most questions use only these four. Learn them by heart.

| Time | Shadow falls | He faces |
|---|---|---|
| Morning | in front | West |
| Morning | behind | East |
| Evening | in front | East |
| Evening | behind | West |

The left and right cases follow from the body map above.

### Shadow and then a movement
Some questions add a walk or a turn. Do it in three steps.

1. Turn the shadow into a compass direction for that time.
2. Turn "towards" or "away from the shadow" into a plain direction.
3. Finish with quarter-turns on the circle North, East, South, West.

Example: evening, a man walks away from his shadow. The shadow points East, so he walks West. He then turns 90 degrees anticlockwise and faces **South**.

> **Watch:** The shadow is not the direction he faces. Read which of the two the question asks for.

patterns.name: Morning shadow
patterns.howToSpot: The time is early morning or sunrise. The shadow is in front, behind, left or right of a person.
steps: Write: morning, shadow West.
Front means he faces West. Behind means he faces East.
Left means he faces North. Right means he faces South.
patterns.why: The shadow is a fixed compass arrow. The person turns to put it on the stated side.

example.q: At sunrise, a man's shadow falls exactly behind him. Which way is he facing?
steps: Morning: the shadow points West.
The shadow is behind him, so he faces the opposite way.
Opposite of West is East.

patterns.name: Evening shadow
patterns.howToSpot: The time is evening or sunset. The shadow is in front, behind, left or right of a person.
steps: Write: evening, shadow East.
Front means he faces East. Behind means he faces West.
Left means he faces South. Right means he faces North.
patterns.why: It is the same rule as morning, with the shadow arrow turned around.

example.q: One evening, Ramesh's shadow falls exactly in front of him. Which way is he facing?
steps: Evening: the shadow points East.
The shadow is in front, so he faces the same way.

patterns.name: Left or right shadow to facing
patterns.howToSpot: The shadow falls to the left or right of the person, and his facing is asked.
steps: Write the shadow direction for that time.
Look at the body map. Find the facing that puts that direction on the stated side.
Check by holding out your hand.
patterns.why: Only one of the four facings puts the shadow on the stated side.

example.q: In the evening, Neha's shadow falls on her left. Which way is she facing?
steps: Evening: the shadow points East.
When she faces South, her left is East.
So she faces South.

patterns.name: Shadow, then a walk or a turn
patterns.howToSpot: The person walks towards or away from the shadow, or turns by 90 or 180 degrees, and the final direction is asked.
steps: Turn the shadow into a compass direction.
Turn 'towards' or 'away' into a direction. Away means the opposite.
Finish the turns with quarter-turns.
patterns.why: After the first step, it is an ordinary final-facing question.

example.q: In the evening, Kiran walks away from his shadow. He then turns 90 degrees anticlockwise. Which way does he face now?
steps: Evening: the shadow points East.
Away from it means he walks West.
Anticlockwise from West is South.

patterns.name: Two people back to back
patterns.howToSpot: Two people stand back to back, and one shadow position is given. The other person's facing or shadow side is asked.
steps: Find the first person's facing from his shadow.
Back to back means the other person faces the opposite way.
Use the body map to place the shadow for the second person.
patterns.why: Back to back fixes the second person's facing at once.

example.q: In the evening, Rohit and Mohit stand back to back. Rohit's shadow falls on his left. Which way does Mohit face?
steps: Evening: the shadow points East. East is on Rohit's left when he faces South.
Mohit faces the opposite way to Rohit.
Opposite of South is North.

revision: Morning: sun East, shadow West. Evening: sun West, shadow East.
Shadow in front: same direction. Shadow behind: opposite direction.
Morning: shadow left means facing North. Shadow right means facing South.
Evening: shadow left means facing South. Shadow right means facing North.
Back to back: the two facings are opposite.
Turn the shadow into a facing, then solve the rest as a normal direction question.

subtopics.title: Position of one point from another
subtopics.concept: Some questions place two people, or a person and a fixed object, on the same map. Put the reference person at the middle of the map first. Then place everyone else, one sentence at a time. The distance and direction between any two people are then read straight off the picture.

formulas.name: Distance between two points
formulas.note: Delta E is the East gap and Delta N is the North gap between the two people.

formulas.name: Distance from speed and time
formulas.note: Use it first when two people walk at different speeds.

tricks.title: Start from the person named after 'from'
tricks.body: For "direction of C from B", draw B first at the middle. The chain then hangs off B. The answer is simply where C lands.

example.q: A is 5 km North of B. C is 5 km East of A. In which direction is C from B?
steps: B at the middle. A is 5 km above B.
C is 5 km to the right of A. So C is 5 East and 5 North of B.

mistakes.wrong: Drawing A first when B is the reference person.
mistakes.right: Put the person named after 'from' at the middle first.

mistakes.wrong: Giving 'C from B' when the question asked 'B from C'.
mistakes.right: Underline the reference person in every sentence.

mistakes.wrong: Adding two distances that need Pythagoras.
mistakes.right: Use the straight-line formula when the two moves are at right angles.

mistakes.wrong: Counting a leg both people walk as part of the gap.
mistakes.right: A shared leg does not change the gap.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing up speed and distance.
mistakes.right: Find distance = speed times time first, then place the person.

subtopics.notes:
### Place the reference first
Two statements can link three people. "C is 5 km East of A. A is 2 km North of B. In which direction is C from B?"

The question asks about **B**. So put B at the middle of the map. Then hang the others on B.

1. B is at the middle.
2. A is 2 km North of B.
3. C is 5 km East of A, so C is 5 km East and 2 km North of B.

C is **North-East** of B.

> **Rule:** Put the person named after "from" at the middle of the map. Everyone else hangs off that person.

### Give every person a position
Put the common start at the middle of the map. Walk each person alone. Write each end point as (East, North).

Example: Amit ends at (3, 4). Sumit ends at (-4, -3). West and South are minus.

### Distance between two people
The gap between two people is the straight line between their two end points.

$$d = \sqrt{(\text{East gap})^2 + (\text{North gap})^2}$$

The East gap is the difference of their East numbers. The North gap is the difference of their North numbers.

Example: Ravi walks 8 km North. Sam walks 15 km East. Ravi is at (0, 8) and Sam is at (15, 0). The gaps are 15 and 8, so the distance is 17 km.

### Direction of one person from another
"Direction of B from A" means: stand at A, look at B. Find the East gap and the North gap from A to B. Read the compass word from their signs.

> **Watch:** "A is East of B" and "B is East of A" give opposite pictures. Underline the person named after "of". That person is the reference.

Reverse the pair and the word flips. If C is North-East of B, then B is South-West of C.

### Shared legs cancel
Suppose both people walk the same leg, such as "then both walk 20 km North". That leg moves both of them by the same amount. It does not change the gap between them.

Example: one walks 9 km East and the other walks 9 km West. Then both walk 20 km North. The gap stays 18 km.

### Chains of positions
"P is 9 km West of Q. Q is 12 km South of R." Start at the last person, R, at the middle of the map. Q is 12 km South of R. P is 9 km West of Q. So P is 9 West and 12 South of R.

Distance from R to P: 9 and 12 give the triple, so 15 km. Direction of P from R: South-West.

### Speed and time
Two people who walk at different speeds move different distances. Distance = speed times time. Then place both on the map.

Example: one walks North at 6 km per hour and the other walks East at 8 km per hour for 2 hours. They are 12 km North and 16 km East. The gap is 20 km.

> **Tip:** Questions often ask "how far and in which direction". Find both. Options often pair the right distance with the wrong direction.

patterns.name: Distance between two walkers
patterns.howToSpot: Two people start from the same place and walk in different directions. The gap between them is asked.
steps: Put the start at the middle of the map.
Find each person's end point as (East, North).
Find the East gap and the North gap.
Use the triples or the square root.
patterns.why: The gap is just the distance between two points on the map.

example.q: Two boys start from the same point. Ravi walks 8 km North and Sam walks 15 km East. How far apart are they?
steps: Ravi is at (0, 8) and Sam is at (15, 0).
The gaps are 15 East and 8 North.
15 and 8 give the triple 8-15-17.

patterns.name: Direction of one person from another
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks in which direction one person is from another after both have walked.
steps: Find both end points from the same start.
Take the reference person as the middle.
Find the East gap and the North gap from the reference to the other person.
Read the compass word from the two signs.
patterns.why: "B from A" is the arrow from A to B, and the signs of the gaps name it.

example.q: From the same point, Meera walks 6 km East and 10 km South. Nisha walks 2 km West and 7 km South. In which direction is Nisha from Meera?
steps: Meera is at (6, -10). Nisha is at (-2, -7).
From Meera to Nisha: 8 km West and 3 km North.
West and North make North-West.

patterns.name: Shared legs
patterns.howToSpot: Both people walk the same leg, or one walks parallel to the other.
steps: Put the two people on the map after their own first legs.
A leg both walk in the same way does not change the gap.
Find the gap after the first legs.
patterns.why: The same leg moves both people equally, so it drops out when you subtract.

example.q: Two friends start together. One walks 9 km East and the other 9 km West. Then both walk 20 km North. How far apart are they?
steps: After the first legs the East gap is 9 + 9 = 18 km.
The 20 km North leg is shared, so the North gap stays 0.
The gap is 18 km.

patterns.name: Chain of positions
patterns.howToSpot: Sentences such as 'A is East of B, B is North of C' link people. The pair not named together is asked.
steps: Put the last person of the chain at the middle.
Add each sentence's move one at a time.
Find the distance and direction of the asked pair.
patterns.why: Chained moves add up like the legs of a walk.

example.q: P is 9 km West of Q. Q is 12 km South of R. How far and in which direction is P from R?
steps: R is at the middle. Q is 12 km South of R.
P is 9 km West of Q, so P is 9 West and 12 South of R.
9 and 12 give 15. West and South make South-West.

patterns.name: Different speeds for the same time
patterns.howToSpot: Two people move at given speeds for some hours. The gap between them is asked.
steps: Find each person's distance = speed times time.
Put both on the map from the common start.
Find the gap from the two positions.
patterns.why: Distance from speed and time turns the question into a plain map problem.

example.q: From a crossing, Ajay cycles North at 6 km per hour and Bala cycles East at 8 km per hour. How far apart are they after 2 hours?
steps: Ajay: $6 \times 2 = 12$ km North.
Bala: $8 \times 2 = 16$ km East.
12 and 16 are 4 times 3 and 4 times 4, so the gap is 4 times 5.

revision: Put the reference person at the middle of the map.
Write each person's end point as (East, North).
Gap: $\sqrt{(\Delta E)^2 + (\Delta N)^2}$.
'B from A': stand at A, look at B. Reversing the pair flips the word.
A leg that both people walk does not change the gap.
Chains: start at the last person and add each move.
Speed times time gives distance.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A person walks along north-south and east-west lines, and you must find how far he is from the start.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Cancel opposite moves and find the net east-west and north-south distance.
Use Pythagoras and look for 3-4-5 or 5-12-13.

example.q: A man walks 9 km East, then 12 km North. How far is he from the start?
example.solution:
The two legs make a right angle
9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225
√225 = 15
Answer: **15 km**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'How much distance did he cover?' for a path with turns.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Distance walked = add all the legs.
Distance from the start is a different thing (the straight line).

example.q: A man walks 3 km East, 4 km North, then 3 km West. How much distance did he cover?
example.solution:
Add all the legs
3 + 4 + 3
The straight distance from the start would be only 4 km
Answer: **10 km**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A person faces some direction, then makes left and right turns.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Draw the turns one by one.
A left turn goes anticlockwise, a right turn goes clockwise.

example.q: Facing South, a man turns left, left and left again. Which way is he facing now?
example.solution:
Facing South, left turn → East
Left turn → North
Left turn → West
Answer: **West**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Direction of the end point from the start
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'In which direction is he from the starting point?'
pyqPatterns.approach:
Find the net east-west and north-south move.
If one of them is zero, the answer is one single direction.

example.q: A man walks 3 km South, 3 km East, then 3 km North. In which direction is he from the start?
example.solution:
North-south: 3 South and 3 North cancel out, so 0
East-west: 3 East
He is straight East of the start
Answer: **East**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Time of day and where a person's shadow falls.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Morning: the sun is in the East, so shadows fall West.
Evening: the sun is in the West, so shadows fall East.

example.q: In the evening, a man's shadow falls in front of him. Which way is he facing?
example.solution:
In the evening the sun is in the West
So the shadow falls towards the East
The shadow is in front, so he faces the same way as the shadow
Answer: **East**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two people walk from one place, and you are asked their distance or direction.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Find the place of each person from the start.
Use the difference between their places for the distance and direction.

example.q: A walks 4 km North and 3 km East. B stays at the start. In which direction is A from B?
example.solution:
B is at the start
A is 3 km East and 4 km North of the start
As both are non-zero, it is a combined direction
Answer: **North-East**

solvedExamples.q: **Ravi walks 3 km towards North, turns right and walks 4 km.** How far is he from the starting point?
solvedExamples.solution: North 3 km, then right (East) 4 km: components (4, 3). Shortest distance = √(4² + 3²) = √25 = **5 km**. (7 km is the distance walked — not asked.)
solvedExamples.shortcut: (3, 4) legs are the 3-4-5 triple — the answer is 5 without computing.
solvedExamples.pattern: shortest distance between start and finish

solvedExamples.q: **Maya walks 5 km South, turns left and walks 3 km, then turns left and walks 5 km.** In which direction is she from the starting point?
solvedExamples.solution: South 5 → (0, −5). Facing South, left = East: +3 → (3, −5). Facing East, left = North: +5 → (3, 0). The y-components cancelled; she is **3 km East** of the start.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Opposite legs of equal length cancel — only the East 3 km survives.
solvedExamples.pattern: direction of the endpoint from start

solvedExamples.q: One morning, a man starts walking and his **shadow falls exactly behind him**. Which direction is he facing?
solvedExamples.solution: In the morning the sun is in the East, so every shadow points **West**. A shadow falling behind him means his back is to the West — he faces **East**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Morning shadow = West; 'behind' ⇒ face opposite the shadow.

solvedExamples.q: **P is 4 km East of Q. R is 3 km South of P.** In which direction is **R from Q**?
solvedExamples.solution: Put Q at the origin: P is (+4, 0), R is (+4, −3). Both x and y components are non-zero, signs (+, −) → **South-East** (exactly 5 km away, by the triple).
solvedExamples.shortcut: Anchor at Q (the asked-from point); R lands in the (+, −) quadrant.

practice.q: **Asha walks 6 m towards East, turns right and walks 8 m.** How far is she from the starting point?
practice.solution: Components (6, 8) = 2 × (3, 4) → distance = 2 × 5 = **10 m**. (14 m is the path walked.)
practice.shortcut: 6-8 is the doubled 3-4 triple → 10.
practice.pattern: shortest distance between start and finish

practice.q: **Vikram walks 9 km towards South, then turns right and walks 12 km.** How far is he from the start?
practice.solution: Components (12, 9) = 3 × (4, 3) → distance = 3 × 5 = **15 km**.
practice.shortcut: 9-12 legs → 15 by the triple; no square root needed.
practice.pattern: shortest distance between start and finish

practice.q: **Neha walks 12 m North, turns right and walks 5 m, then turns right and walks 12 m.** How far is she from the starting point?
practice.solution: North 12 and South 12 cancel completely; only the East 5 m remains → **5 m**. (29 m is the total distance walked.)
practice.shortcut: Equal out-and-back legs on one axis vanish; only the crosswise leg survives.
practice.pattern: shortest distance between start and finish

practice.q: A man facing **West turns 90° clockwise, then 180° anticlockwise**. Which direction is he facing now?
practice.solution: West --90° clockwise--> North --180°--> **South**. A 180° turn flips the heading whatever its sense.
practice.shortcut: Write the heading after each turn: W → N → S.

practice.q: **A is 5 km North of B. C is 5 km East of A.** In which direction is **C from B**?
practice.solution: B at origin → A at (0, 5) → C at (5, 5). Both components positive → **North-East** of B (7.07 km away, if asked).
practice.shortcut: Chain from B, the asked-from point: up 5, right 5 → NE.

practice.q: **Sameer walks 8 km East, then 6 km West, then 3 km East.** How far is he from the starting point?
practice.solution: Net East = 8 − 6 + 3 = 5 km; net North–South = 0 → **5 km East**. (17 km is the walking total.)
practice.shortcut: One signed column for East-West; opposite directions subtract.
practice.pattern: shortest distance between start and finish

practice.q: In the **evening**, Ramesh's shadow falls **exactly in front of him**. Which direction is he facing?
practice.solution: Evening sun is in the West, so shadows point **East**. A shadow in front means he faces along it → **East**.
practice.shortcut: Evening shadow = East; 'in front' ⇒ facing the shadow's direction.

practice.q: **Facing South, Sita walks 4 km, turns left and walks 4 km, then turns left again and walks 4 km.** In which direction is her endpoint from the start?
practice.solution: South 4 → (0, −4). Facing South, left = East → (4, −4). Facing East, left = North → (4, 0). Net: **4 km East**.
practice.shortcut: The two South-North legs cancel; the middle leg decides.
practice.pattern: direction of the endpoint from start

practice.q: Two friends start from the same point. **X walks 3 km North and then 4 km East. Y walks 4 km South and then 3 km West.** How far apart are they now?
practice.shortcut: Both walkers from the same origin; subtract components, then Pythagoras (√98 = 7√2).

practice.q: **Kiran starts facing East and walks 5 km, turns right and walks 3 km, turns right and walks 5 km, then turns right again and walks 2 km.** In which direction is she from the starting point?
practice.solution: East 5 → (5, 0); right → South 3 → (5, −3); right → West 5 → (0, −3); right → North 2 → (0, −1). The x-components cancel; 1 km of Southward drift remains → **South** of the start.
practice.shortcut: Cancel East-West first (5 and 5); the leftover South 1 km decides the direction.
practice.pattern: direction of the endpoint from start

practice.q: One morning, Amit walks **10 m towards the rising sun**, then turns left and walks 10 m. In which direction is he from his starting point?
practice.solution: Rising sun = East: he walks 10 m East, then turns left (facing East, left = North) 10 m. Endpoint (10, 10) → **North-East** of the start.
practice.shortcut: Sunrise = East; facing East, left is North — (+, +) endpoint means North-East.

practice.q: **Rani walks 7 km North, turns right and walks 7 km East, then turns right and walks 7 km South.** What is her position relative to the start?
practice.solution: North 7 and South 7 cancel; the East 7 km survives → she is **7 km East** of the start. (21 km is the distance walked.)
practice.shortcut: Out-and-back legs cancel; only the middle leg counts.
practice.pattern: direction of the endpoint from start

practice.q: **Imran walks 5 km North, turns right and walks 3 km, then turns right again and walks 9 km.** How far is he from the starting point?
practice.solution: North 5 → (0, 5); right = East 3 → (3, 5); right = South 9 → (3, −4). Distance = √(9 + 16) = **5 km**.
practice.shortcut: Components (3, 4) reappear after cancellation → the triple gives 5.
practice.pattern: shortest distance between start and finish

practice.q: **D is 6 km West of C. C is 4 km South of B.** In which direction is **B from D**?
practice.solution: Place D at the origin. 'D is 6 km West of C' puts C 6 km **East** of D. 'C is 4 km South of B' puts B 4 km **North** of C. So B sits at (+6, +4) from D → **North-East** of D.
practice.shortcut: Anchor at D (the asked-from point); C hangs East, B hangs North of C.

practice.q: A soldier marching towards **North** is ordered **'about turn'**, and then **'right turn'**. In which direction is he marching now?
practice.solution: About turn: North → South. Right turn from South: South → **West** (right-hand cycle N→E→S→W).
practice.shortcut: About turn = +180°; right turn = +90° on the N→E→S→W cycle.

practice.q: **Ravi walks 3 km East, then turns and walks 4 km North. How far is he from his starting point?**
practice.solution: Net legs: (3 E, 4 N). Shortest distance = $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=\sqrt{25}$ = **5 km** — the 3-4-5 triple.
practice.shortcut: Spot the triple 3-4-5 and answer without computing.

practice.q: **A man walks 5 km North, then 5 km South, then 3 km East. How far is he from his starting point?**
practice.solution: The 5 N and 5 S legs cancel completely. Only the 3 km East leg survives → he is **3 km** from the start.
practice.shortcut: Cancel opposite legs first; whatever survives is the answer.

practice.q: **A man walks 5√2 km North-East, then 5√2 km North-West. How far is he from his starting point?**
practice.solution: 5√2 NE = 5 N + 5 E; 5√2 NW = 5 N + 5 W. East and West cancel → net 10 km North → **10 km** from the start.
practice.shortcut: k√2 on a diagonal splits into k + k on the two component directions.

practice.q: **A woman walks 3 km East and then 4 km North. What is the total distance she has covered?**
practice.solution: 'Total distance covered' adds every leg: 3 + 4 = **7 km**. (5 km is the shortest distance from the start — a different question with a planted option.)
practice.shortcut: 'Covered' = add the legs; 'away from start' = Pythagoras.

practice.q: **A man walks 6 km East, then 6 km North, then 12 km South. How far is he from his starting point?**
practice.solution: Net legs: 6 E; North: 6 − 12 = −6 (net 6 South). Distance = $\sqrt{6^2+6^2}$ = **6√2 km**.
practice.shortcut: 6-6 legs at right angles → hypotenuse is leg×√2.

practice.q: **Sunita walks 10 km East, then 4 km North, then 10 km West. How far is she from her starting point?**
practice.solution: 10 E and 10 W cancel → net 4 km North. She is **4 km** from the start.
practice.shortcut: Mirror legs East-West cancel; only the North leg remains.

practice.q: **A man walks 2√2 km South-East, then 2 km South. How far is he from his starting point?**
practice.solution: 2√2 SE = 2 S + 2 E. Add the extra 2 S → net (2 E, 4 S). Distance = $\sqrt{4+16}=\sqrt{20}$ = **2√5 km**.
practice.shortcut: Split the diagonal, net the axes, keep the root unsimplified like the options.

practice.q: **A man is facing West. He turns 90° anticlockwise, then 270° clockwise. Which direction is he facing now?**
practice.solution: Quarters: anticlockwise 90° = −1, clockwise 270° = +3. Net = +2 quarter turns. W + 2 (on the cycle W → N → E) = **East**.
practice.shortcut: Add turns as quarter turns (right +, left −) before touching the compass.

practice.q: **A woman walks 4 km North, then 3 km East. In which direction is she from her starting point?**
practice.solution: Net (3 E, 4 N): both components positive → the endpoint sits in the **North-East** quadrant of the start.
practice.shortcut: Net the legs; both nonzero → combined compass word.

practice.q: **Walking North, Ravi walks 5 km, turns left and walks 5 km, then turns left again and walks 5 km. In which direction is his final position from his starting point?**
practice.solution: Facing N: left → walks 5 W; left again → walks 5 S. Endpoint: 5 W and 5 N − 5 S = 5 N → (5 W, 5 N) → **North-West** of the start.
practice.shortcut: Each 'left' rotates the walking arrow 90° anticlockwise; draw one arrow per leg.

practice.q: **A man walks 6 km East, then turns back and walks 2 km. Which direction is he facing now, and how far is he from his start?**
practice.solution: Turning back flips his facing East → **West**. Position: 6 − 2 = 4 km East of the start. So: West, 4 km.
practice.shortcut: A 180° turn flips facing and cancels distance along the same line.

practice.q: **Facing South, a man turns 90° to his left three times. Which direction is he facing now?**
practice.solution: Each left = −1 quarter turn; net −3 ≡ +1 (mod 4). S + 1 clockwise step (S → W) = **West**.
practice.shortcut: Three lefts = one right; S + one right step = West.

practice.q: **A man walks 3 km South, then 3 km East, then 3 km North. In which direction is his final position from his starting point?**
practice.solution: Net legs: South 3 and North 3 cancel; 3 km East remains → the endpoint is due **East** of the start.
practice.shortcut: The S-N pair cancels; only the East leg describes the endpoint.

practice.q: **Facing East, a man takes two right turns and then one left turn. Which direction is he facing at the end?**
practice.solution: Net = +2 − 1 = +1 quarter turn. E + 1 clockwise step (E → S) = **South**.
practice.shortcut: Right-right-left = one right; E then one clockwise step = South.

practice.q: **Early in the morning, Ravi walks towards his shadow. In which direction is he walking?**
practice.solution: Morning sun is in the East, so every shadow points **West**. Walking towards his shadow = walking West.
practice.shortcut: Morning: sun East → shadow West. The anchor first, always.

practice.q: **Early morning, Amit stands facing his shadow. He then turns 90° clockwise. Which direction is he facing now?**
practice.solution: Morning shadow = West; facing his shadow = facing West. One clockwise quarter turn: W → **North**.
practice.shortcut: Decode the shadow to a facing first; then it is a plain turn question.

practice.q: **In the morning, Manish's shadow falls exactly to his right. Which direction is he facing?**
practice.solution: Morning shadow = West. Facing South, the right hand points West — so the shadow (West) falls to his right → he faces **South**.
practice.shortcut: Body map: face South → right is West (morning's shadow side).

practice.q: **In the morning, a man's shadow falls exactly in front of him. He then turns through 180°. Which direction is he facing now?**
practice.solution: Morning shadow = West; in front of him → he was facing West. A 180° turn flips him to **East**.
practice.shortcut: Shadow in front → facing opposite the shadow; then flip for 180°.

practice.q: **At sunset, Priya and Amit stand back to back. Priya's shadow falls exactly on Amit. In which direction is Amit facing?**
practice.solution: Sunset shadows point **East**, so Amit stands East of Priya. Back to back means they face opposite directions; Priya faces Amit (East), so Amit faces **West**.
practice.shortcut: Shadow lands on the friend → friend is on the shadow side; back to back → opposite facings.

practice.q: **Early morning, a man's shadow falls exactly to his left. Which direction is he facing?**
practice.solution: Morning shadow = West. Facing North, the left hand points West — so the shadow falls to his left → he faces **North**.
practice.shortcut: Body map: face North → left is West (morning's shadow side).

practice.q: **In the evening, Kiran's shadow falls exactly behind her. Which direction is she facing?**
practice.solution: Evening shadows point **East**. The shadow is behind her, so she faces the opposite → **West**.
practice.shortcut: Evening: shadow East; behind → face West.

practice.q: **Early morning, Ramesh sees his shadow in front of him and walks 10 steps towards it. He then turns through 180° and walks 4 steps. In which direction is he facing at the end?**
practice.solution: Morning shadow = West; in front → he faced West and walked 10 steps West. The 180° turn flips him to face **East** (he is now 6 steps West of his start).
practice.shortcut: The 180° turn decides the facing; the steps only fix the position.

practice.q: **At sunrise, Sita's shadow falls exactly behind her. She turns 90° to her right. Which direction is she facing now?**
practice.solution: Sunrise shadow = West; it falls behind her, so she faced East. One right (clockwise) turn: E → **South**.
practice.shortcut: Behind-shadow at sunrise = facing East; then one clockwise step to South.

practice.q: **In the evening, Vijay's shadow falls exactly to his left. Which direction is he facing?**
practice.solution: Evening shadow = East. Facing South, the left hand points East — so the shadow falls to his left → he faces **South**.
practice.shortcut: Body map: face South → left is East (evening's shadow side).

practice.q: **Amit walks 3 km East and then 4 km North. Sumit walks 4 km West and then 3 km South from the same starting point. How far apart are they?**
practice.solution: Amit is at (3 E, 4 N); Sumit at (4 W, 3 S). Gap = $\sqrt{(3+4)^2+(4+3)^2}=\sqrt{98}=7\sqrt2\approx$ **9.9 km**.
practice.shortcut: Walk each to coordinates, subtract, Pythagoras.

practice.q: **A man walks 4 km North and 3 km East from his house while his wife stays at home. In which direction is the man from his wife?**
practice.solution: The man is at (3 E, 4 N) from home. Both components positive → **North-East** of his wife.
practice.shortcut: One person fixed = origin; read the compass word of the walker's coordinates.

practice.q: **Two friends start from the same point. One walks 5 km North and the other 5 km South; then both walk 12 km East. How far apart are they now?**
practice.solution: The shared 12 km East shifts both equally — it changes nothing. They sit 5 + 5 = **10 km** apart on the North-South line.
practice.shortcut: Equal shared legs cancel in the gap; only the opposing legs count.

practice.q: **P walks 6 km East and then 8 km South. Q walks 6 km West and then 8 km North from the same starting point. In which direction is Q from P?**
practice.solution: P = (6 E, 8 S); Q = (6 W, 8 N). From P to Q: ΔE = −12 (West), ΔN = +16 (North) → **North-West**.
practice.shortcut: 'Q from P' = stand at P; the arrow to Q has both components — combine the words.

practice.q: **X starts from point A and walks 5 km North. Y starts from point B, which is 5 km East of A, and also walks 5 km North. How far apart are X and Y now?**
practice.solution: X = (0, 5); Y = (5, 5). The equal 5 km North legs cancel in the gap; only the fixed 5 km East offset remains → **5 km**.
practice.shortcut: Identical legs cancel; the starting offset is the whole answer.

practice.q: **From her house, Renu walks 12 km South and then 5 km West. How far is she from her house?**
practice.shortcut: 5-12-13 is the 3-4-5 family: spot it and skip the root.

practice.q: **Meena walks 2 km North, then 2 km East, then 2 km North again. In which direction is she from her starting point?**
practice.solution: Net (2 E, 4 N): both components positive → **North-East** (more North than East, but still the NE quadrant).
practice.shortcut: Unequal legs still give the quadrant word; magnitudes don't change it.

practice.q: **One pole stands 3 km East and 4 km South of a well. Another stands 3 km West and 4 km South of the same well. How far apart are the two poles?**
practice.solution: Pole 1 = (3 E, 4 S); pole 2 = (3 W, 4 S). The 4 km South is shared → gap = 3 + 3 = **6 km** on the East-West line.
practice.shortcut: Same offset on one axis → the gap is just the other axis's difference.

practice.q: **Sameer walks 5 km East, then 5 km North, then 5 km West. In which direction is he now from his starting point?**
practice.solution: 5 E and 5 W cancel → net (0, 5): due **North** of the start. (North-West needs a leftover West component — there is none.)
practice.shortcut: Cancel first, then name the word — 'North-West' is the trap when E-W cancel exactly.

practice.q: **A man walks 6 km North and then 8 km East to reach his office. How much shorter would his trip be if a straight road joined his home to the office?**
practice.solution: Straight road = $\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10$ km. Actual trip = 6 + 8 = 14 km. Saving = 14 − 10 = **4 km**.
practice.shortcut: 'How much shorter' = total − displacement; both numbers appear as decoy options.

practice.q: **Walking East, Asha turns right and walks 4 km, then turns right again and walks 4 km. Which direction was her last leg?**
practice.solution: Facing E: right turn → South; right again → West. Her last leg ran **West**.
practice.shortcut: Each right turn moves the arrow one step clockwise: E → S → W.

practice.q: **A man walks 8 km North; realising he took a wrong path, he turns back and walks 3 km, then turns right and walks 4 km. Which direction is he facing at the end?**
practice.solution: The about-turn flips him from North-facing to South-facing. A right turn from South points him **West** — he walks the last leg facing West.
practice.shortcut: Retrace = face opposite; apply the next turn from the flipped facing.

practice.q: **A is 5 km East of B, and B is 12 km North of C. How far and in which direction is A from C?**
practice.solution: Put C at the origin: B = (0, 12), A = (5, 12). Gap = $\sqrt{5^2+12^2}$ = 13 km, and (5 E, 12 N) points **North-East** → 13 km North-East.
practice.shortcut: Chain the offsets from the last person; then one Pythagoras plus a compass word.

practice.q: **An office is 4 km South of a mall, and the mall is 3 km East of a park. How far and in which direction is the office from the park?**
practice.solution: Park at the origin: mall = (3 E, 0), office = (3 E, 4 S). Gap = $\sqrt{9+16}$ = 5 km, direction (3 E, 4 S) → **South-East**.
practice.shortcut: Stack the offsets in order, then read the pair (number + word) as one answer.
